title: Angles, sine and cosine
summary: What sin, cos and arcsin do, degrees vs radians, measuring from the normal, and why arcsin of a number above 1 means total internal reflection.

diagrams.title: Sine and cosine on the unit circle
diagrams.tryThis: Drag the angle from 0° to 90° and watch sin grow from 0 to 1 while cos shrinks from 1 to 0; then try arcsin of 1.2.

checks.prompt: Snell’s law gives $\sin\theta_t = 0.5$. What is θₜ in degrees?
hints: Make sure your calculator is in degree mode.

checks.prompt: A ray crosses a 100 µm layer at 20° from the normal. How long is its path through the layer (in µm)?
hints: Draw the right-angled triangle: thickness is the side next to the angle.
cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse, so hypotenuse = d / cos θ.
solution: The thickness is adjacent to the angle; the path is the hypotenuse.

checks.prompt: Going from silicon into air, Snell’s law asks for $\sin\theta_t = 1.2$. What does that mean?

options.text: There is no refracted ray: the light is totally internally reflected.
options.feedback: Correct: sin never exceeds 1, so no angle satisfies Snell’s law. All light is reflected.

options.text: θₜ = 90°, the ray skims the surface.
options.feedback: That happens exactly at sin θₜ = 1 (the critical angle). Beyond it there is no refracted ray at all.

options.text: My calculator is in radians; switching to degrees will fix it.
options.feedback: The unit mode doesn’t change the fact that sin cannot exceed 1.
arcsin(1.2) does not exist: sine values lie between −1 and 1.

hints: What is the largest value sin θ can take?
If no angle fits, where does the light go?
solution: sin θ is always between −1 and 1, so no refracted ray exists.
The light is totally reflected back into the silicon: total internal reflection.
